CHINA PRESS, FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 13, 1936.

Radio Artists
File Protest
Against Ban

Local Entertainers Ask
Telegraph Office To
Reconsider Ruling

9 UNIONS SEND
JOINT PETITION

New Broadcast Decrees
Proclaimed By Ministry
Of Communications

Recent restrictions placed on their radio programs by the Shanghai Telegraph Office of the Ministry of Communications have brought forth another storm of protests from some 300 local air entertainers. Facing the threat of unemployment because some of their most popular acts have either been banned or taken off the best radio time, the broadcasters have petitioned the Telegraph Office executives to reconsider the ruling.

According to information obtained here yesterday, the entertainers, represented by nine different unions, have merged their organizations in the present fight, in order that their appeal will carry more weight with Telegraph Office officials. A special committee has been organized by leading entertainers to study programs which are affected by the ban.

Follow July Ruling

The present protests arose out of the ruling proclaimed here July 1, when programs bordering on immorality were ordered from the air by the censor board. This board, consisting of representatives from the Telegraph Office and the Bureaus of Social Affairs and Education, has been keeping a close watch on all the programs which go on the air. Broadcasters, according to the ruling, are required to submit the drafts of their skits, plays, announcements and other entertainment material for examination before the programs are released by the stations.

The restriction proclaimed by the Ministry officials specified that entertainment items listed under nine headings should not be included in radio broadcast of any particular station for a total time of more than two hours each day. The period from 1 to 10 p.m. which is looked upon by station managers as the "best radio time," is closed to entertainment program included in the "ban" list.

Among the items on which the censors are keeping a close watch are the popular Soochow, Yangchow, Shanghai, and other native acts. These programs, the Ministry officials believe, are often indecent.

No Action Expected

The executives of the local Telegraph Office are not expected to take any action on the protest of the entertainers. Mr. Orlando Pan, General Manager of the Office, told a reporter yesterday that he is waiting for the new broadcasting regulation recently proclaimed in Nanking by the Ministry of Communications.

These rulings, advance information indicates, are considerably more drastic than the censor regulations now in effect. While details of the Ministry's order are not yet available in Shanghai, it is understood that the time of each broadcasting station will be allotted proportionately to entertainment, educational, and other programs. The skits and plays now on the ban list are likely to have an extremely small place in the new schedule of the Ministry.

交通部颁布
新的广播法令

交通部上海电政局最近对其广播节目施加的限制，引发了约300名本地空中艺人的另一轮抗议风暴。由于他们一些最受欢迎的节目要么被禁播，要么被移出最佳广播时段，面临失业威胁，广播从业者已 petition 电政局高管重新考虑该裁决。

根据昨日在此获得的消息，由九个不同工会代表的艺人们在此次抗争中合并了他们的组织，以便他们的诉求在电政局官员面前更有分量。主要艺人已组织一个特别委员会，研究受禁令影响的节目。

遵循七月裁决

目前的抗议源于7月1日在此颁布的裁决，当时审查委员会下令禁止播放涉及不道德内容的节目。该委员会由电政局以及社会局和教育局的代表组成，一直密切关注所有播出节目。根据该裁决，广播从业者在电台发布节目之前，必须提交短剧、戏剧、公告和其他娱乐材料的草稿以供审查。

交通部官员颁布的限制规定，列在九个项目下的娱乐内容，在任何特定电台的每日广播总时长不得超过两小时。被电台经理视为“最佳广播时段”的晚上1点至10点，禁止播放列入“禁令”名单的娱乐节目。

审查人员密切关注的节目包括流行的苏州、扬州、上海及其他地方曲艺节目。交通部官员认为，这些节目往往有不雅之处。

预计不会采取行动

本地电政局高管预计不会对艺人的抗议采取任何行动。该局总经理潘奥尔兰多先生（Mr. Orlando Pan，音译）昨日告诉记者，他正在等待交通部最近在南京颁布的新广播法规。

预先获得的信息表明，这些裁决比现行审查规定严厉得多。虽然交通部命令的细节尚未在上海公布，但据悉，各广播电台的时间将按比例分配给娱乐、教育和其他节目。目前在禁令名单上的短剧和戏剧在新时间表中所占比例可能极小。

Movietone (電聲) Weekly:

NEW FILM CENSORSHIP REGULATIONS

The Central Film Censorship Committee has promulgated a set of new regulations one of which stipulates that no advertisements of a moving picture may be published in newspapers before the film company had secured from the Committee approval of the film and a certificate for its showing.

The following measures governing fines for violation of these regulations have also been drawn up:-
1) A fine of $60 will be imposed for a first offence.
2) A fine of $120 will be imposed for a second offence.
3) A fine of $240 will be imposed for a third offence.
4) A fine of $480 will be imposed for a fourth offence.
For a fifth offence, the Committee will refuse to censor films of the company concerned.

According to the Central Film Censorship Committee, the imposition of fines was intended as a restriction directed specially against foreign owned motion picture companies. Chinese pictures the manuscripts of which have been passed by the preliminary censorship are exempted from these restrictions.

Pao Pao (報報) dated July 16 (comment):

"PROPER IN NAME AND AGREEABLE IN WORDS"

Since the introduction of radios into Shanghai, many broadcasting stations in Shanghai have been broadcasting licentious songs. This is harmful to morals and is being constantly suppressed by the authorities.

Some days ago, a certain evening newspaper published a report on the banning of certain broadcasting programmes. The following was the newspaper report:-

"Since the enforcement of the inspection and adjustment of broadcasting programmes by the Shanghai Telegraph Bureau of the Ministry of Communications, the manuscripts sent by the station for inspection are strictly censored. This is intended to promote the knowledge of the people and to be of aid to education. If anything improper is found, the broadcasting will be either prohibited or be given a time limit to make alterations. Songs like the 'New Life Pao Chuan' (新生活卷) etc. will naturally be allowed. However, the 'May 30 Tragedy' (五卅慘案) has been altered to 'Nanking Road in the Month of May' (五月之南京路); the 'May 3 Incident' (五三) to 'An Account of the Negotiations'; and 'September 18 Incident' (九一八) to 'An Account of the Lost Territory' (失地記). The names and words thus altered are all very proper and agreeable."

We can understand a ban on licentious songs in broadcasting, but we cannot understand what good can be produced by alteration of the titles as mentioned above.

People say that the weakness and eventual annihilation of a race are due to foreign aggression; but they do not realize that a measure such as that relating to broadcasting given above is one of the principal causes.

新的电影审查条例

4) 四犯者罚款480元。

据中央电影检查委员会称，实施罚款旨在特别限制外资电影公司。经初步审查通过剧本的中国影片不受这些限制的约束。

7月16日《报报》（评论）：

“名正言顺”

自从收音机引入上海以来，上海的许多广播电台一直在播放淫秽歌曲。这有害于道德风尚，当局一直在不断予以取缔。

日前，某晚报刊登了一篇关于禁止某些广播节目的报道。该报报道如下：-

“自从交通部上海电报局实施对广播节目的检查和调整后，各电台送审的稿件受到严格审查。此举旨在增进民众知识并辅助教育。若发现不当内容，要么禁止广播，要么限定时间进行修改。像《新生活卷》等歌曲自然会被允许。然而，《五卅惨案》被改为《五月之南京路》；《五三》改为《交涉记》；《九一八》改为《失地记》。如此修改后的名称和措辞都非常得体且顺耳。”

我们可以理解禁止广播中的淫秽歌曲，但我们无法理解上述标题的修改能产生什么好处。

人们说，一个种族的衰弱乃至最终灭亡是由于外国侵略所致；但他们没有意识到，上述有关广播的措施正是主要原因之一。

THE BANNING OF CERTAIN PLAYS.

The "Shun Pao" publishes the following letter sent by the Shanghai Municipality Vocational Circles National Salvation Association to the Zuh Nyi Small Drama Group(實戰小劇場) :-
"Recently, the S.M.C. unreasonably interfered with the staging of certain patriotic plays by your Group. This action on the part of the S.M.C. is regarded by this Association as harmful to the prestige of China and as contempt of international treaties. This Association pledges SUPPORT to your Group with the full strength of its entire body of members and hopes your Group will continue the struggle for justice so as to overcome the evil influences and to remove the obstacles to the national emancipation movement."

China Times published the following comment on July 4 :-

The Broadcasting Programmes

Something was said on July 3 about the suppression of certain broadcasting programmes, but as this was incomplete, we offer the following explanations:-
As a result of repeated prohibition and strict censorship, many broadcasting programmes which would cause the hair of listeners to stand on end have been suppressed. However, some broadcasting programmes include such songs as "my darling", etc, while songs of national salvation are never broadcasted. (Is it because the broadcasting of patriotic songs would affect the diplomatic relations of the country? This has caused us to ask: in what way does the Chinese people's movement to save their country affect the diplomatic relations of the country?)
As a time limit has been placed upon the broadcasting of "Tai-Huang" (黃) and "Sien-Chuen" (仙傳) (Stories), the time for the broadcasting of dramatic songs has been, therefore, increased. But what will be done after this? Is the object of this increase in the time for the broadcasting of dramatic songs to enable the people to listen to songs of love such as "my darling", etc.?
Readers will recollect that not long ago a dramatic play entitled "The Smuggling" which the "Hai-Yen" (海燕) Dramatic Society had intended to broadcast was unreasonably prohibited by the S.M.C. Up to the present, the International Telegraph Administration has not made any protest against this arbitrary prohibition. We are at a loss to understand why the scenario of a play which had been previously censored and approved by the authorities should have been suppressed by the Council and no protest should have been made against this interference.
On our part, we hope that strict measures will be adopted to suppress or limit the broadcasting of immoral programmes, but if it is discovered that only the manner of broadcasting programmes is improper, the International Telegraph Administration should not fail to rectify it instead of resorting to suppression only. It is also to be hoped that the Administration will render prompt protection to those whose programmes are beneficial to the people in case they meet with outside interference or oppression. Unless this is done, the promotion of education by means of radio broadcasting will prove a failure.
It is to be hoped that the above points will receive the favourable consideration of the authorities .

禁止某些剧目。

《申报》刊登了上海市职业界救国会发给“實戰小劇場”（Zuh Nyi Small Drama Group，音译）的一封信：-
“近期，工部局无理干涉贵团上演某些爱国剧目。本会认为工部局的这一行动有损中国威望，且蔑视国际条约。本会誓以全体会员之力支持贵团，并希望贵团继续为正义而斗争，以克服邪恶影响，扫除民族解放运动的障碍。”

7月4日《China Times》（字林西报/中文报纸名待考，此处依惯例暂译为中国时报）发表如下评论：-

广播节目

7月3日曾提及取缔某些广播节目一事，但因所述不全，现作如下解释：-
由于反复禁止和严格审查，许多令听众毛骨悚然的广播节目已被取缔。然而，一些广播节目仍包含如“我的亲爱的”等歌曲，而救亡歌曲却从未播出。（难道是因为播出爱国歌曲会影响国家的外交关系吗？这让我们不禁要问：中国人民的救国运动究竟在哪些方面影响了国家的外交关系？）
由于对《太黄》（Tai-Huang）和《仙传》（Sien-Chuen）（故事）的广播设定了时限，因此戏剧歌曲的广播时间得以增加。但这之后又会如何呢？增加戏剧歌曲广播时间的目的，难道是为了让民众聆听如“我的亲爱的”等爱情歌曲吗？
读者们还记得，不久前，“海燕”剧社打算广播的一出名为《走私》的话剧，被工部局无理禁止。截至目前，国际电信管理局并未对这种任意禁止提出任何抗议。我们不解的是，为何一部剧本此前已经过当局审查并批准，却仍被公董局取缔，且对此类干涉未提出任何抗议。
就我方而言，我们希望采取严厉措施取缔或限制不道德节目的广播，但如果发现仅仅是广播节目的方式不当，国际电信管理局不应仅采取取缔手段，而应予以纠正。同时也希望管理局对那些有益于民众的节目在遭遇外部干涉或压迫时给予及时保护。若不如此，通过无线电广播促进教育的努力将以失败告终。
希望上述几点能得到当局的有利考虑。

July 2, 1936. Afternoon Translation.

Sin Wan Pao and other local newspapers :-

RE-ADJUSTMENT OF PROGRAMMES OF BROADCASTING STATIONS

Upon receiving instructions to control local broadcasting stations, the Chinese Telegraph Administration of the Ministry of Communications has re-adjusted wave lengths, examined the manuscripts of songs and stories and made inquiries about the announcers of broadcasting stations.
The Telegraph Administration has now laid down the following measures governing programmes of people's broadcasting stations in Shanghai :-
Of late certain local broadcasting stations have been broadcasting obscene songs. This is harmful to the morals of the people. For this reason, the Chinese Telegraph Administration has commenced the examination of manuscripts of songs and assumed control over broadcasting. Over 1,000 manuscripts of songs have been examined and some have been amended, whilst others have been banned.
The Administration has drawn up the following rules regarding the programme of a broadcasting station :-
1) The theme of the songs and stories must be clear.
2) Songs or stories must not constitute a danger to peace and order.
3) Songs or stories should be in accordance with Kuomintang doctrines.
4) No obscene songs or stories are to be broadcasted.
5) Songs or stories should not deal with mythology or superstition.
6) Songs or stories should not violate scientific theories.
7) They should not violate ethics.
8) They should not be vulgar.
9) They should not propagate feudal thoughts.
Any broadcasting station that violates these rules will be suppressed. The broadcasting of Ningpo "Tai Huang" is absolutely prohibited.
During the examination, numerous songs were found unsuitable and in some cases a time limit was set for proper changes to be made. Improvements were introduced in the following:- Shanghai "Tai Huang", comic songs or stories, Soochow "Tai Huang", Ningpo Story telling, songs, Kompo plays and Soochow story telling.
The broadcasting of gramophone records is dealt with in a similar manner. A broadcasting station may function not more than three hours a day. Between 7 and 10 p.m. every day no broadcasting is allowed for the people must have rest.
It has been found that the songs or stories broadcasted are not in accordance with the manuscripts that have been examined. Therefore, the Telegraph Administration has elected supervisors to listen daily to the programmes of all broadcasting stations.
The Central Broadcasting Control Office has published a broadcasting weekly in which the plays and stories that have been approved will be given. In order to elevate the minds of the people, the Telegraph Administration is buying Kuomintang songs and gramophone records which will be lent out to all broadcasting stations free of charge.
The Administration is inquiring into the number of announcers in the employ of broadcasting stations. A registration of announcers will be enforced.

《新闻报》及其他本地报纸：-

广播电台节目的重新调整

交通部中华电信管理局在接到控制本地广播电台的指令后，重新调整了波长，审查了歌曲和故事的稿件，并对广播电台的播音员进行了调查。
电信管理局现已制定以下管理上海人民广播电台节目的措施：-
近来，某些本地广播电台播放淫秽歌曲。这有害于民众道德。为此，中华电信管理局已开始审查歌曲稿件并接管广播控制权。已审查了1000多份歌曲稿件，部分进行了修改，部分被禁止。
管理局制定了以下关于广播电台节目的规则：-
1) 歌曲和故事的主题必须清晰。
2) 歌曲或故事不得危害和平与秩序。
3) 歌曲或故事应符合国民党主义。
4) 不得广播淫秽歌曲或故事。
5) 歌曲或故事不得涉及神话或迷信。
6) 歌曲或故事不得违背科学理论。
7) 不得违背伦理道德。
8) 不得庸俗。
9) 不得宣扬封建思想。
任何违反这些规则的广播电台将被取缔。绝对禁止广播宁波“太黄”。
在审查过程中，发现许多歌曲不合适，在某些情况下限定了适当修改的时间。以下方面得到了改进：上海“太黄”、滑稽歌曲或故事、苏州“太黄”、宁波评弹、歌曲、Kompo（音译）戏剧和苏州评话。
唱片广播也以类似方式处理。广播电台每天运作不得超过三小时。每晚7点至10点之间不允许广播，因为民众需要休息。
经查，播出的歌曲或故事与已审查的稿件不符。因此，电信管理局选派了监督员，每天收听所有广播电台的节目。
中央广播管制办公室出版了一份广播周刊，其中将列出已批准的剧目和故事。为了提升民众的思想境界，电信管理局正在购买国民党歌曲和唱片，并将免费借给所有广播电台。
管理局正在调查各广播电台雇用的播音员人数。将实行播音员登记制度。

COMPLAINT AGAINST TELEPHONE COMPANY

Yesterday lawyer Tung Yui (董俞) sent the following letter to the Shanghai Special District Telephone Question Committee:-
"Despite the fact that I had paid on June 1 my telephone charges for the month of May, the Shanghai Telephone Company included this amount in my June account. Fortunately the error was rectified after I had found the bill for the month of May. The action of the Shanghai Telephone Company in deliberately making a false charge in my bill with the intention of making a double collection is indeed unreasonable and savours of trickery and extortion. This clearly shows a lack of business morals on the part of the Shanghai Telephone Company. I am sending you this letter and the two bills with a request that your Committee will open strong negotiations with the Shanghai Telephone Company."

Ta Kung Pao (Correspondence from Tsinan) :-

MURDER OF A JAPANESE AT TSINAN

On the night of June 23, a Japanese named Ando, manager of the Shinwa Yoko at Tsinan, was attacked with axes by five drug smugglers and killed. His wife and his servant, a Chinese named Wang Chi Yen (王濟元), were injured. The Shantung Provincial Government has issued a reward of $2,000 for the arrest of the murderers and has issued an order that the accused be arrested within ten days.
The Special Detective Squad has made exhaustive enquiries and has arrested four of the five principal offenders and many accomplices. All the arrested persons were sent to the Bureau of Public Safety on June 29.

After the Shanghai Telegraph Bureau took over

《字林西报》及其他本地报纸：-

广播节目

自交通部下令由上海电报局接管上海所有商业广播电台的管理权以来，该局不遗余力地推行改进措施。
由于部分广播电台的节目包含淫秽内容，该局已通知各广播电台，自7月1日起，所有节目的稿件必须事先提交该局审查，未经该局批准的节目不得播出。此外，对某些类型的戏剧和歌曲的播出时段也进行了限制。
据悉，众多从事各类娱乐广播的人士已按照指示提交了节目副本。该局将这些节目全部送交上海教育局和社会局审议。稿件审查工作将在月底前完成。
有时多个长篇节目同时播出，因此广播人员发现难以准备三份节目副本，并已请求电报局通融。据说，该局将允许他们仅提交节目大纲以供审查，省略对白及次要部分。该局官员将在节目播出时通过监听进行核查。

March 6, 1 36. Afternoon translation.

Central China Daily News (telephone from Nanking)

THE CHINESE GOVERNMENT & BROADCASTING STATIONS

According to an official connected with the
radio administration, the following five matters relating
to the readjustment of radio broadcasting have been
rectified during the past two years.

1. With a view to putting a stop to troubles arising out
of wave lengths, the apparatus of radio broadcasting
stations were investigated and 13 radio broadcasting
stations in Shanghai were suppressed for violation
of regulations.

2. The programmes of the radio stations were censored.
A radio station to maintain supervision on radio
broadcasting stations will be established in Shanghai.

3. Besides the radio stations which have been established
at Peiping and Shanghai, a big radio station will be
erected at Chungking.

4. In order to maintain the sovereignty of China, private
radio stations belonging to foreigners will be suppressed.

5. 70,000 owners of radio receivers have been registered.

1936年3月6日。午后译件。

《华中日报》（南京电话通讯）

中国政府与广播电台

据一位与无线电管理部门有关的官员称，过去两年中，以下五项关于无线电广播调整的事项已得到整顿。

1. 为制止因波长引起的纠纷，对广播电台的设备进行了调查，上海有13家广播电台因违规而被取缔。

2. 对广播电台的节目进行了审查。将在上海设立一个无线电管理机构，以监督广播电台。

3. 除已在北平和上海设立的广播电台外，还将在重庆建立一座大型广播电台。

4. 为维护中国主权，属于外国人的私人广播电台将被取缔。

5. 已登记了70,000名无线电接收机所有者。

November 22, 1935. Morning Translation.

World Morning News (世界晨報) published the following comment on November 21:-

Ronins of a certain country are instigating traitorous merchants to hoard silver dollars and subsidiary coins. As a result, the value of silver coins has gone up.

Traitorous merchants select the markets as their chief source for obtaining silver coins. They then try to smuggle these coins abroad. Hawkers in the markets must refrain from selling silver dollars and subsidiary coins to these traitorous merchants for the consideration of a discount.

Chen Pao (Shanghai Morning Post) and other local newspapers:

WANG CHING WEI ARRIVES IN SHANGHAI

Wang Ching Wei, President of the Executive Yuan, left the Central Hospital at Nanking on November 20. In company with his wife and Dr. Chu Min Nyi, Chief Secretary of the Executive Yuan, President Wang arrived in Shanghai at 8 a.m. yesterday by train.

Interviewed by our reporter, Dr. Chu Min Nyi made the following statements:-

"President Wang Ching Wei, who was confined in the Central Hospital for 19 days, is gradually recovering his health. He has come to Shanghai to undergo X Ray to ascertain whether or not it will be necessary to take out the bullet from his back. This morning (November 21), Dr. Now and Dr. Noll examined President Wang's injuries. It is probable that he will require a rest for about three months in order to recover his health".

China Times and other local newspapers:-

BUREAU OF SOCIAL AFFAIRS TO SUPPRESS ABSURD PROGRAMMES OF BROADCASTING STATIONS

Chang Ping Hwa (張平華), Chief of the 4th Department of the Bureau of Social Affairs, in an interview with a reporter of the Sing Sung News Agency yesterday, made the following statement regarding the endeavours of the Bureau to suppress absurd broadcasting in Shanghai:-

"Various business concerns are conducting propaganda through broadcasting stations. With a view to pleasing those people among the public who have low tastes and ideals, the broadcasting stations used to include in their programmes absurd and nonsensical matters and ballads of a degenerate character. As such matters are bound to cause people to become inert, and mentally ruined, the Bureau of Social Affairs together with the Bureau of Education have devised measures to suppress them.

"According to these measures, only programmes relating to education and social knowledge are to be broadcasted in the morning; proper amusement programmes, however, may be given in the afternoon and evening."

汪精卫抵沪

行政院院长汪精卫于11月20日离开南京中央医院。汪院长在其夫人及行政院秘书长褚民谊博士的陪同下，于昨日上午8时乘火车抵达上海。

褚民谊博士在接受本报记者采访时发表了如下声明：-

“汪精卫院长在中央医院住院19天后，健康状况逐渐恢复。他此次来沪是为了进行X光检查，以确定是否有必要取出背部的子弹。今晨（11月21日），Now医生和Noll医生检查了汪院长的伤势。他可能需要休息约三个月以恢复健康”。

《字林西报》及其他本地报纸：-

社会局将取缔广播电台的荒诞节目

社会局第四科科长张平华（Chang Ping Hwa）昨日在接受《星生通讯社》记者采访时，就社会局取缔上海荒诞广播的努力发表了如下声明：-

“各家商行正通过广播电台进行宣传。为了迎合公众中品味和理想低俗的人群，广播电台以往在节目中包含荒诞无稽的内容和颓废性质的歌谣。鉴于此类内容必然导致人们精神懈怠和心智败坏，社会局会同教育局制定了取缔措施。

“根据这些措施，上午仅允许播出与教育和社会知识相关的节目；而适当的娱乐节目则可在下午和晚间播出。”

Jul 24, 1939
THE CHINA WEEKLY REVIEW
99

the Japanese army is accomplishing for the benefit of
the Chinese people, and how, through its heroic efforts,
the British and other foreigners have been restrained
from enslaving the entire Chinese population.
Needless to say, stations ZQHA and XOJB have
to pay their announcers more than most other stations,
for it is obviously a severe strain on the commentator's
conscience, especially since the Japanese stations require
that Chinese deliver to Chinese, and foreigners deliver
to foreigners full accounts of the Japanese "good will"
mission in China.
Besides those mouthpieces and a few other smaller
owned stations, which they have coerced into doing
their bidding, the Japanese have still another (unofficial)
spokesman, or spokeswoman rather, in the person of
Mrs. Robertson, who broadcasts the news of the pro-
Japanese Shanghai Times over station ZQHA (820 kc),
owned and operated by Mrs. Robertson herself.
Two stations which cause Major Asano and his
Japanese Control Board more sleepless nights than all
the others put together, are stations XMHC and XMHA,
which are the most powerful stations in Shanghai. Both
are under American control and thus are outside the
jurisdiction of his "Control Board." Station XMHC
is owned by the Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury and ex-
presses the sympathetic Chinese policy of the paper in its
news broadcasts to a far greater public than the paper
could ever hope to reach. More deleterious to Japanese
military objectives is the fact that it broadcasts in Chinese
the news of its Chinese paper the Ta Mei Wan Pao, the
morning edition of which had been recently suspended
from publication by the S.M.C. as a result of Japanese
pressure, and police "appeasement."
Station XMHA is the property of an American,
U.S. Harkson, who is proprietor of the Henningsen
Produce Company, dealers in eggs, egg products, butter
and manufactureres of ice cream and confectionery.
The most provocative thing about this station, so far as
the Japanese are concerned, aside from the fact that they
do not control it, is the news broadcast of Carol Alcott.
As a news commentator he is by far the most popular
among the foreign population of Shanghai, and what
makes him popular among the foreigners and Chinese
makes him bitterly unpopular with the Japanese Control
Board and its Nipponese army supporters. The Japanese
claim that Alcott's broadcasts are "pro-British," and
as such are anathema to the Nipponese point of view.
Whether the Japanese will be able to finally get
Alcott off the air or curb his broadcasts remains to be
seen. Recently there have been rumors of trouble
between Alcott and the manager of the station who,
allegedly did not approve of some of Alcott's state-
ments. Several weeks ago the Japanese succeeded by
pressure, intimidation and chicanery in causing the Harkson
station to discontinue the broadcasts of The China Weekly
Review, whose weekly summaries of world news equalled
Alcott's daily news broadcasts in popularity among
both foreigners and Chinese. Several hundred protests,
more than 100 in writing, were received as a result of
the discontinuance of The Review's broadcast and as
a result, the manager of XMHA, fearing a loss in prestige
of his station, tried to induce the The Review to resume,
but subject to censorship as to its utterances. The
editor of The Review rejected this offer.
Since XMHA is the property of the Henningsen
interests and is primarily useful to them as an advertising
medium for their butter, ice cream and confectionery
products, it remains to be seen how far they may be wil-
ling to go in opposing Japanese control. The main Hen-
ningsen plant is said to be located in Japanese-controlled
territory, hence subject to military pressure.
The Henningsen station recently has been criticised
for its failure to re-broadcast here the independent news
and entertainment program of the famous Treasure
Island Station at San Francisco. The Treasure Island
Station (W6XBE) was constructed and is maintained
by the General Electric Company (without advertising)
for the purpose of maintaining American news and
cultural contacts with South American and Oriental
countries. Its broadcasts may be picked up here by
shortwave receivers between 7:30 A.M. and 11 A. M.,
and 8 P.M. to 11 P.M. If the programs were re-broad-
cast by a local station they could be heard by every owner
of a radio in east and central China.
It must be remembered of course, that radio, as an
instrument of propaganda is almost limitless, in comparison
with other agencies of communication. News and com-
ment which might not be so disastrous to the Japanese
interests in Shanghai, where practically everyone is of
the same mind concerning their invasion, might be
exceedingly inflammatory in those places where the
Japanese are struggling to keep out all the truth—that
truth which they have good reason to believe, might
prove to be as disastrous an invasion for their despotism,
as the one they had envisioned for China.
For entertainment, XHMC and XMHA depend up-
on recordings, giving the public anything from Beethoven
to the latest song hits, which are often quite a bit late
by the time they arrive in Shanghai. The Christian
Broadcasting Station, station XMHD (760 kc.) is devoted
almost exclusively to religious topics, with the exception
of news comments and occasional musical recordings.
Indeed if an embargo were ever placed on records, the
whole radio industry of Shanghai would collapse over-
night with a completeness that no strategy or edict of
the Japanese Control Board could ever hope to perform.
Not a single Shanghai station has had sufficient enter-
prise or ingenuity to build up its own programs as sta-
tions in the United States, even in small towns, have done.
The police Department of the S.M.C. has its own
station through which it directs the activities of its six
armoured volunteer cars and its dozen or so normal
radio vans, which patrol the streets. The S.M.C. it-
self also had in mind the erection of a radio station with
which to advance the music of its municipal orchestra,
but having allocated $200,000 for the orchestra and
only $3000 or so for the radio, all logical accountancy,
I suppose, collapsed at this point, and with it the broad-
casting project.
Thus into the surcharged air of Shanghai, goes
all the confusing network of sound, all the secret code
messages and dispatches from the private stations of the
various consulates, and military headquarters, the buz-
zing and interceptions of the Japanese, and so forth.
Shanghai is said to have more radio stations than any
other city in the world, a fact that one can prove any-
time by simply spinning the dial of his radio.
Today, radio in Shanghai as at present constituted
can see little or nothing, now or in the future, but a dreary
prospect, and cannot fail but reflect the anxiety and ten-
sion of these hectic days. And even those stations beyond
control of the Japanese Control Board, XMHA and
XMHC, in a position to give this city and the
other cities of China which they cover, outspoken views
and facts, may soon have to face a new delima and
persecution. Already the Japanese have in the process
of construction two kilowatt transmitters, now half
completed, and probably ready for operation next month.
These transmitters, allegedly were designed exclusively
to jam XMHA and XMHC off the air permanently,
if they choose to ignore the Control Board's last and
final ultimatum.
The real test will come when the Japanese seriously
try to force Alcott off the air as they succeeded in doing
with The China Weekly Review's weekly summary of world
news. Up to the present Alcott, who also is Shanghai's
best police reporter, has had S.M.P. support, although
a Japanese terrorist once threw a bomb against the front
door of XMHC while he was broadcasting and black-
mailers have written him numerous threatening letters.

1939年7月24日
《密勒氏评论报》
99

日军正在为中国人民的福祉而成就大业，以及通过其英勇努力，英国人和其他外国人如何被阻止奴役全体中国人口。
不用说，ZQHA 和 XOJB 电台不得不向其播音员支付高于大多数其他电台的薪酬，因为这对评论员的良心显然是一种严峻的考验，尤其是因为日方电台要求中国人向中国人、外国人向外国人全面传达日本在华“善意”使命的内容。
除了那些喉舌机构以及少数几家被胁迫听命于日方的小型私营电台外，日本人还有另一位（非官方的）代言人，或者更确切地说是女代言人，即罗伯逊夫人（Mrs. Robertson），她通过 ZQHA 电台（820 千周）广播亲日的《上海泰晤士报》（Shanghai Times）的新闻，该电台由罗伯逊夫人本人拥有并经营。
令浅野少校（Major Asano）及其日本管制委员会比其他所有情况加起来都更加失眠的两家电台，是 XMHC 和 XMHA 电台，它们是上海功率最强的两家电台。两者均受美国人控制，因此不在其“管制委员会”的管辖范围内。XMHC 电台由《上海晚邮报与水星报》（Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury）拥有，并在其新闻广播中表达该报同情中国的政策，其受众范围远超该报本身所能企及。对日军军事目标更具破坏性的是，该电台用中文广播其中文报纸《大美晚报》的新闻，该报晨版最近因日本人的压力和工部局警务处的“绥靖”而被公共租界工部局（S.M.C.）勒令停刊。
XMHA 电台归美国人 U.S. Harkson（音译）所有，他是亨宁森农产品公司（Henningsen Produce Company）的所有者，该公司经销鸡蛋、蛋制品、黄油，并制造冰淇淋和糖果。就日本人而言，这家电台最具挑衅性的地方，除了他们无法控制它这一事实外，还在于卡罗尔·奥尔科特（Carol Alcott）的新闻广播。作为一名新闻评论员，他在上海外籍人口中极受欢迎，而使他受到外国人和中国人欢迎的因素，也使他遭到日本管制委员会及其日本军队支持者的强烈憎恶。日本人声称奥尔科特的广播“亲英”，因此从日本人的观点来看是大逆不道的。
日本人最终能否让奥尔科特停播或限制其广播，仍有待观察。最近有传言称奥尔科特与电台经理之间发生纠纷，据称经理不赞同奥尔科特的某些言论。几周前，日本人通过施压、恐吓和欺诈手段，迫使哈克森（Harkson）的电台停止广播《密勒氏评论报》，该报的世界新闻每周摘要在外国人和中国人中的受欢迎程度堪比奥尔科特的每日新闻广播。由于《评论报》广播的中断，收到了数百起抗议，其中书面抗议超过100起，因此，XMHA 电台经理担心电台声誉受损，试图诱导《评论报》恢复广播，但要求其言论接受审查。《评论报》编辑拒绝了这一提议。
由于 XMHA 电台属于亨宁森财团（Henningsen interests）的财产，且主要作为其黄油、冰淇淋和糖果产品的广告媒介对其有用，因此他们在反对日本控制方面愿意走多远，仍有待观察。据悉，亨宁森的主要工厂位于日本控制的领土内，因此易受军事压力影响。
亨宁森电台最近因其未能在此重播旧金山著名的宝藏岛电台（Treasure Island Station）的独立新闻和娱乐节目而受到批评。宝藏岛电台（W6XBE）由通用电气公司（General Electric Company）建造并维护（无广告），旨在维持美国与南美及东方国家的新闻和文化联系。其广播可在上午 7:30 至 11:00 以及晚上 8:00 至 11:00 之间通过短波接收机在此收听到。如果由本地电台重播这些节目，中国东部和中部地区的每一位收音机所有者都能听到。
当然，必须记住，与其他传播机构相比，无线电作为宣传工具几乎是无限的。在上海，几乎所有人都对日本的入侵持相同看法，某些新闻和评论可能对日本在上海的利益不会造成太大灾难，但在那些日本人极力掩盖真相的地方，这些内容可能会极具煽动性——他们有充分理由相信，这种真相的传播对其专制统治来说，可能证明是一场与他们曾设想加诸中国的那场入侵同样灾难性的入侵。
在娱乐方面，XHMC 和 XMHA 依赖唱片，向公众提供从贝多芬到最新流行歌曲的各种内容，这些歌曲传到上海时往往已经滞后不少。基督教广播电台 XMHD（760 千周）几乎专门致力于宗教话题，例外情况仅有新闻评论和偶尔的音乐唱片播放。的确，如果对唱片实施禁运，整个上海无线电行业将一夜之间彻底崩溃，其彻底程度是日本管制委员会的任何策略或法令都无法企及的。没有一家上海电台拥有足够的进取心或独创性来建立自己的节目，就像美国甚至小城镇的电台所做的那样。
公共租界工部局（S.M.C.）警务处拥有自己的电台，通过该电台指挥其六辆装甲志愿人员汽车和十几辆普通无线电巡逻车的活动，这些车辆在街道上巡逻。工部局本身也曾考虑建立一座广播电台，以推广其市立交响乐团的音乐，但在为乐团拨款 200,000 美元而仅为无线电拨款约 3,000 美元后，我想，所有合理的会计核算在此刻都崩溃了，广播计划也随之搁浅。
因此，在上海充满电荷的空气中，充斥着所有令人困惑的声音网络、来自各领事馆和军事总部私人电台的所有秘密代码信息和电报、日本人的嗡嗡声和拦截等等。据说上海的电台数量比世界上任何其他城市都多，任何人只需转动收音机的调谐旋钮即可随时证实这一事实。
如今，上海目前的无线电状况，无论现在还是将来，都看不到什么希望，前景黯淡，不可避免地反映出这些动荡日子中的焦虑和紧张。甚至那些不受日本管制委员会控制的电台，即 XMHA 和 XMHC，虽然有能力向这座城市及其覆盖的中国其他城市提供坦率的观点和事实，但可能很快就要面临新的困境和迫害。日本人已经在建造两台千瓦发射机，目前已完成一半，可能下个月即可投入运行。据称，如果这些电台选择无视管制委员会的最后通牒，这些发射机将专门用于永久干扰 XMHA 和 XMHC 使其停播。
真正的考验将是当日本人认真试图迫使奥尔科特停播时，正如他们成功迫使《密勒氏评论报》停止世界新闻每周摘要那样。到目前为止，奥尔科特（他也是上海最好的警务记者）一直得到上海公共租界工部局警务处（S.M.P.）的支持，尽管一名日本恐怖分子曾在他广播期间向 XMHC 的前门投掷炸弹，勒索者也给他写过许多威胁信。

The Shanghai Broadcasting Situation and Future Prospects
(EDITORIAL CORRESPONDENCE)

FOLLOWING Japanese penetration into Shanghai, radio broadcasting suffered the disintegration and chaos that most businesses have experienced. In line with their general policy of suppression and disruption, a Japanese Control Board was established in March, 1938 with the sole aim of liquidating all stations not in complete accord with their imperialistic designs and the mission of a "New Order" (or rather disorder) in Asia. The control Board was given the convenient misnomer, "Japanese Broadcasting Superintendence office," located in Hardoon building and under the guidance of a Major Asano. "Superintendence" in this instance meant anything from direct interference to outright confiscation of station equipment and material.

Today, after two years, radio broadcasting has revived somewhat, if the number of stations operating is an indication of revival—but it exists in a tense and apprehensive atmosphere. Without exception all Chinese stations have "lost their voice" with which they had previously contributed to the defense and rebuilding of a new China. Before outbreak of war in 1937, there existed thirty-five privately owned Chinese stations, five foreign ones and two government stations. While there had been some governmental restriction from Nanking, the stations in the International Settlement and French Concession operated with a degree of independence and integrity which they probably will not enjoy again as long as the Japanese Control Board remains in Shanghai. For the most part, the erection of a radio station did not involve a great deal of capital, and a fairly good station could be built from $8,000 to $20,000, Chinese currency. They could be located in a loft or, as was most common, in a private house or store. Radio in Shanghai was never a spectacular affair such as it is in American and European cities even of less magnitude and population. The regulation and control of radio broadcasting in Shanghai prior to the Japanese occupation was vested in the Ministry of Communications of the National Government at Nanking. Sometime in December, 1936, a board of censorship for the regulation and control of programs was set up by the Ministry of Communications.

After the outbreak of the war and throughout the fighting here the Chinese stations naturally espoused the cause of Nationalist China militantly. They saturated their commercial programs with appeals and propaganda on behalf of their soldiers who were desperately defending Shanghai. Even after the retreat of the Chinese army, most of the stations continued (their appeals and voiced their solidarity with their country's struggle. The Japanese of course could not countenance this, so long after all semblance of propaganda had vanished from commercial broadcasting of the Chinese stations, the Japanese continued reprisals and suppressions. There was more in this policy than mere retaliation: it was evident to the Japanese militarists, as it is to all dictatorial forces, that radio is one of the most potent forms of propaganda. So long as it was beyond their control, it was an everlasting menace to their designs. Their sole objective was to supplant all stations by ones of their own control.

Desiring to give as little pretext as possible to the Japanese, the Shanghai Municipal Council forbade Chinese stations within the International Settlement from broadcasting any propaganda whatsoever. This "appeasement" policy of the S.M.C. was not so much the fault of the Council itself as it was the vacillating policies of the governments, which theoretically control the council. The French Concession, allowed no interference from the Japanese Control Board, and though no new stations were permitted establishment, those already within the Concession enjoyed a certain degree of immunity and license.

The first thing the Japanese Control Board did was to dispatch three trucks and confiscate for their own purposes the two government station—one of which, now XOJB, operating on a frequency of 900 kc continues to perpetrate upon the ears of Chinese and foreigners alike most flagrant Nipponese propaganda. They have programs in Cantonese, Mandarin and English, using Domei reports for their news broadcasts. The Chinese programs are extremely anti-British. As for the British, Americans and other foreign listeners the Japanese seemingly take pains not to offend their intelligence too much.

After the seizure the Japanese Control Board, immediately sent an ultimatum, in the form of a memorandum to all radio stations advising them that the Control Board had taken over all matters regarding supervision, direction and suppression of broadcasting, which formerly was under the jurisdiction of the National government. A week or so later, another memorandum was dispatched to all stations stating that permission had to be obtained from the Control Board before any station could commence operation and instructing all stations then in existence to forward to the board before April 15 their permits that had been issued to them by the Ministry of Communications of the Chinese government. The stations generally ignored this memorandum. Thoroughly incensed, the Control Board waited until April 20 and then issued Memo No. 3., stating that if the stations failed to register before April 27, they would be considered as having abandoned all privileges, rights of protection.

Apprehensive over these threats, the local station owners held a meeting. The chairman was delegated to request the S.M.C. to deal justly with the matter and afford them whatever protection it could. They stated their willingness to register with the Police Department of the S.M.C. and were prepared to furnish whatever guarantees necessary, toward sustaining the peace, abstaining from propaganda or any remarks which might be objectionable to the sensitive natures of the invaders. But the station owners should be given credit for almost unanimity in one thing—they would rather close their station than suffer humiliating control by the Japanese.

Realizing the formidable opposition to his control board, Major Asano, tried to assure them that the "superintendence" office would not exceed the form of control previously exercised by the Kuomintang government except insofar as anti-Japanese propaganda was concerned, and moreover it was the intention of the Board to protect the acquired rights of all stations then in existence.

As a result of hysteria, six of the twenty-one Chinese owned stations finally registered with the Control Board, and the day following the expiration of the last ultimatum, all the remaining Chinese stations closed down. A few days later however a total of eight Chinese owned stations resumed broadcasting.

During these days the S.M.C. was forced to yield many points as a result of Japanese threats. The Police Department "outlawed" all anti-Japanese propaganda from Chinese stations, but still the Japanese were not

上海广播业现状与未来展望
（读者来信）

继日军侵入上海之后，无线电广播业遭受了大多数企业所经历的瓦解与混乱。按照其镇压和破坏的总体政策，日本于1938年3月成立了一个管制委员会，其唯一目的是清算所有不完全符合其帝国主义图谋以及在亚洲建立“新秩序”（或者更确切地说是“无秩序”）使命的电台。该管制委员会被冠以方便但名不副实的称呼——“日本广播监理处”，设于哈同大楼（Hardoon building），由浅野少校（Major Asano）指导。在此情形下，“监理”意味着从直接干涉到公然没收电台设备和材料等一切行为。

两年后的今天，如果以运营电台的数量作为复兴的指标，无线电广播业已有所复苏——但它存在于一种紧张和忧虑的氛围中。无一例外，所有中国电台都失去了它们此前为保卫和重建新中国所贡献的“声音”。在1937年战争爆发前，存在三十五家私营中国电台、五家外国电台和两家政府电台。虽然南京方面曾有一些政府限制，但在公共租界和法租界的电台享有某种程度的独立性和正直性，只要日本管制委员会仍驻留上海，这种独立性和正直性恐怕将不复存在。大体而言，建立一家广播电台并不涉及大量资本，建造一家相当不错的电台只需花费8,000至20,000元法币。电台可以设在阁楼里，或者像最常见的情况那样，设在私人住宅或商店内。上海的广播业从未像在美国和欧洲城市（即使是规模和人口较小的城市）那样成为一种引人注目的事业。在日本占领之前，上海无线电广播的监管和控制权归属于南京国民政府交通部。1936年12月的某个时候，交通部设立了一个审查委员会，用于监管和控制节目。

战争爆发后及在上海战斗期间，中国电台自然坚定地拥护国民中国的事业。它们的商业节目中充斥着为其拼命保卫上海的士兵进行的呼吁和宣传。即使在中国军队撤退后，大多数电台仍继续（其呼吁并表达对其国家斗争的声援。日本人当然不能容忍这一点，所以尽管中国电台的商业广播中所有宣传的痕迹都已消失，日本人仍继续进行报复和镇压。这一政策不仅仅是报复：对于日本军国主义者来说，正如对所有独裁势力一样，显而易见的是，无线电是最有力的宣传形式之一。只要它超出他们的控制范围，就对其图谋构成永恒的威胁。他们的唯一目标是用由其控制的电台取代所有其他电台。

为了尽可能不给日本人提供借口，上海公共租界工部局禁止公共租界内的中国电台播放任何宣传内容。工部局的这种“绥靖”政策与其说是工部局本身的过错，不如说是理论上控制工部局的各国政府摇摆不定政策的后果。法租界不允许日本管制委员会进行干涉，虽然不允许设立新电台，但已在租界内的电台享有一定程度的豁免权和自由。

日本管制委员会做的第一件事是派出三辆卡车，出于自身目的没收了两家政府电台——其中一家即现在的XOJB，在900千周频率上运营，持续向中国人和外国人的耳朵灌输最露骨的日本宣传。他们设有粤语、国语和英语节目，新闻广播使用同盟社（Domei）的报道。中文节目极具反英色彩。至于英国人、美国人和其他外国听众，日本人似乎小心翼翼地不过分冒犯他们的智力。

接管后，日本管制委员会立即以备忘录的形式向所有电台发出最后通牒，告知他们管制委员会已接管所有关于广播监督、指导和镇压的事务，这些事务以前属于国民政府的管辖范围。大约一周后，又向所有电台发送了一份备忘录，声明任何电台在开始运营前必须获得管制委员会的许可，并指示当时存在的所有电台在4月15日前将其由中国政府交通部颁发的许可证提交给委员会。各电台普遍忽视了这份备忘录。管制委员会彻底被激怒，等到4月20日发布了第3号备忘录，声明如果电台在4月27日前未注册，将被视为放弃所有特权和保护权。

出于对这些威胁的担忧，本地电台业主举行了一次会议。主席受委托请求工部局公正处理此事，并提供其所能提供的任何保护。他们表示愿意向工部局警务处注册，并准备提供维持和平、不进行宣传或发表任何可能冒犯入侵者敏感神经的言论所需的任何保证。但电台业主们在一点上几乎一致，值得称赞——他们宁愿关闭电台，也不愿忍受日本的屈辱控制。

意识到其管制委员会面临强大的反对，浅野少校试图向他们保证，“监理”办公室不会超越国民党政府以前行使的控制形式，除非涉及反日宣传，此外，委员会的意图是保护当时所有现存电台的既得权利。

由于恐慌，二十一家的中国私营电台中有六家最终在管制委员会注册，而在最后一次最后通牒过期的第二天，所有剩余的中国电台均停业。然而几天后，共有八家中国私营电台恢复广播。

在这些日子里，由于日本的威胁，工部局被迫在许多问题上让步。警务处“取缔”了中国电台的所有反日宣传，但日本人仍然不

satisfied. They agreed to negotiate and while the negotiations were proceeding the S.M.C. promised to issue no new permits, this being precisely what the Japanese wanted. Chinese desiring to install new stations had to approach the Japanese Control Board. Finally, the S.M.C. agreed to permit no new stations in the International Settlement without Japanese permission. Following this, the stations which had registered with the Japanese Control Board were constantly faced with new afflictions and coercions. For no sooner had a Chinese owned station registered with the Board, than pressure was exerted upon it to convert it into an instrument of Nipponese propaganda.

Those stations which still remained adamant to the ultimatums, had to suffer further reprisals. Having ignored a last warning to appear at the Control Board and register, the Hwa Tung, Dah Loh Tung Fang and Fuh Ying stations were notified that they had forfeited their rights to broadcast, and that their respective wavelengths were being allocated to certain Japanese and foreign station which had seen fit to register. The Fuh Ying (Pure Karma Buddhist Association) had refused to register because the proprietors felt that the religious nature of their broadcasts rendered them immune to military and all other temporal control. They were neither a commercial or political station and their programs consisted entirely of prayers and chants. However the Japanese, remaining impervious to their protests, started station XQMW on the same wavelength 980 kc to "jam" out the Buddhist station which had been operating on 980 kc for a considerable period.

The policy of jamming out unfavorable broadcasts has been a consistent practice of the Japanese, and has been one of their principle devices to effect control. In this instance, they simply shoved one station upon another's wavelength, so that the two stations, in being heard together, became nothing but a series of distorted sounds. The Japanese have done this in many cases, for example, XHHR, the Lai Tung station, was forced to assume 840 kc. to jam XHHU, the Dah Chung Hwa station, which had been operated on the same frequency in the French Concession, and which, because of this had felt no necessity for registering with the Japanese. The Mei Sung (XQMS kc 1220) was established to nullify the Tung Fang XHHG, one of the most adamant opponents of Japanese control.

But the Japanese Superintendence Office did not confine its persecution to Chinese owned stations. The foreign owned stations came in for their share of intimidation, and in the case of XMHE, an American Commercial Station, it took the form of a direct and unveiled attempt to get it off the air. The American station was registered with the American Consulate-General, being the property of an American, P.H. Vanmeter. As 780 kc was then vacant, he chose this frequency for his station. Subsequently, he was informed by the Japanese Control Board that his station had been changed to 800 kc. However, 800 kc was the wavelength of the Sun Sun station, which had not registered. Compliance with this order being impossible, it was of course, ignored, and the American station continued on 780 kc. Shortly afterwards, station XHHV, the Yeu Lien, announced that it was returning to the air on a wavelength of 780 kc, this frequency being assigned to it by Major Asano. The Yeu Lien had been closed for many months, and the only condition upon which it was allowed to reopen was that it become an agent in the Board's warfare against the American station. Following still more complications, station XMHE is now operating on a wavelength of 720 kc.

Besides using one station to jam another off the air, the Control Board maintains five 100 to 200 watt transmitters for interference only. On these they put a

"buzzer," which is designed to make a jumble of noise, which some say, incidentally, is about as intelligible as most Japanese propaganda. The Japanese also have a pleasant habit of backing their trucks up to any Chinese station in the International Settlement which does not submit to their commands, and siezing their equipment outright. The police offer no resistence to this high-handed action.

This summary provides but a small background, indicative of the obstacles which have been placed in the way of radio development in Shanghai. However, despite these difficulties there are today 41 commercial broadcasting stations in the city. Some of them are duplicates, others in doubtful condition, and all of them, dependent upon their own resources are hard pressed to continue in operation. Advertising, which is the life-blood of radio, is extremely meager, and whatever there is, is ridiculously cheap. It is actually possible to get an hour per day on a leading station at the rate of $350 (Chinese) per month or a "spot" announcement for as low as $37.50 per month. Rates such as these cannot be expected to induce any startling originality in radio broadcasts or enable the employment of talent for public entertainment. As a result of insufficiency of income it is imperative, especially for the foreign owned stations to limit themselves almost exclusively to recordings, with only one or two announcers at most, and a daily news commentator. The Chinese stations which comprise the bulk have studio presentations at various times, but these stations have been rendered so innocuous by control and regimentation, that their programs have little appeal even for their own people, whose anxiety and resentment leaves them in a poor frame of mind for censored entertainment.

The programs that might interest the Chinese populations, that is those coming by short wave from the National Government Station in Chungking, are constantly being intercepted and "jammed" by the vigilant Japanese. Sometimes however there comes a welcome discussion in Chinese in the form of programs by "roving" stations, which must of course, remain as hidden here as they do in Germany. These are the spontaneous creations of alert Chinese in Shanghai and constitute their contributions to their country's struggle. On these programs, national hymns are played, recruits summoned, and the aims and struggles of the National Government and leaders voiced.

The two Japanese stations XQHA (630 kc) and XOJB (900 ck) receive financial assistance from their government, hence ought to be able to give better programs than they do. But in view of what the Japanese have done in other fields it would be taxing the imagination too much to expect them to exert themselves overmuch in spreading their culture over the radio, particularly in view of the obvious fact that the Japanese radio stations, like everything else, are under the close control of the army authorities.

While Tokyo has a "culture" bureau in the Foreign Office and spends vast sums in the propagation of Nipponese culture abroad, the Japanese warlords who are in control here have little or no interest in such things.

Station XQHA does rebroadcast some Tokio programs which it feels might meet with the approval of Shanghai (and the army authorities). Its propaganda and news is "tuned" to this level and no higher. The music is almost exclusively recordings, although programs sometimes consist of German and Italian operas sung in Japanese. The other main Japanese station, XOJB, was formerly the Chinese government Civic Center station. After its confiscation, it became headquarters for Japanese army radio propaganda in Shanghai broadcasting in Mandarin, Cantonese and English. The propaganda, as in the other station, comes in the form of elaborate news detailing the miraculous things which

感到满意。他们同意进行谈判，而在谈判进行期间，工部局（S.M.C.）承诺不颁发新的许可证，这正是日本人所希望的。希望安装新电台的中国人不得不向日本管制委员会接洽。最终，工部局同意未经日本许可，不在国际租界内批准任何新电台。此后，那些已在日本管制委员会注册的电台不断面临新的折磨和胁迫。中国拥有的电台一旦在委员会注册，随即就受到压力，迫使其转变为日本宣传的工具。

那些对最后通牒仍持强硬态度的电台，不得不遭受进一步的报复。华通（Hwa Tung）、大罗东方（Dah Loh Tung Fang）和福英（Fuh Ying）电台无视前往管制委员会注册的最后警告，被通知已丧失广播权，其各自波长正被分配给某些认为适宜注册的日本及外国电台。福英（纯 karma 佛教协会）拒绝注册，因为业主认为其广播的宗教性质使其免受军事及一切世俗控制。他们既非商业电台也非政治电台，其节目完全由祈祷和诵经组成。然而，日本人对其抗议置若罔闻，在同一波长 980 kc 上启动了 XQMW 电台，以“干扰”那家已在 980 kc 上运营相当长一段时间的佛教电台。

干扰不利广播的政策一直是日本人的一贯做法，也是其实施控制的主要手段之一。在这种情况下，他们 simply 将一个电台强加到另一个电台的波长上，使得两个电台同时被收听时，变成了一系列失真的声音。日本人在许多案例中都这样做过，例如，来通电台（Lai Tung station，呼号 XHHR）被迫改用 840 kc，以干扰大中华电台（Dah Chung Hwa station，呼号 XHHU），后者一直在法租界以相同频率运营，并因此认为没有必要向日本人注册。美声电台（Mei Sung，呼号 XQMS，频率 1220 kc）的设立旨在抵消东方电台（Tung Fang，呼号 XHHG），后者是日本控制最坚定的反对者之一。

但日本监理处（Superintendence Office）的迫害并不局限于中国拥有的电台。外资电台也遭受了不同程度的恐吓，在美商电台 XMHE 的案例中，这种恐吓表现为直接且毫不掩饰地试图使其停播。该美国电台在美国总领事馆注册，系美国人 P.H. Vanmeter 的财产。由于当时 780 kc 空闲，他选择此频率作为其电台频率。随后，他接到日本管制委员会的通知，称其电台频率已改为 800 kc。然而，800 kc 是未注册的孙孙电台（Sun Sun station）的波长。由于无法遵守此命令，该通知自然被忽略，美国电台继续在 780 kc 上运营。不久之后，友联电台（Yeu Lien，呼号 XHHV）宣布将以 780 kc 的波长恢复广播，该频率由浅野少校（Major Asano）分配给它。友联电台已关闭数月，其获准重新开放的唯一条件是成为委员会对抗美国电台斗争中的代理人。经过更多复杂的纠葛后，XMHE 电台目前在 720 kc 波长上运营。

除了利用一个电台干扰另一个电台使其停播外，管制委员会还维持着五台功率为 100 至 200 瓦的发射机，专门用于干扰。他们在这些发射机上使用一种“蜂鸣器”，旨在制造一团噪音，顺便说一句，有人说这种噪音的可懂度大约与大多数日本宣传相当。日本人还有一个令人“愉快”的习惯，即将卡车倒靠在国际租界内任何不服从其命令的中国电台旁，并公然没收其设备。警察对这种蛮横行为不加抵抗。

本概要仅提供了一小部分背景，说明了上海无线电发展所面临的障碍。然而，尽管存在这些困难，目前市内仍有 41 家商业广播电台。其中一些是重复的，另一些状况可疑，而且所有电台都依赖自身资源，难以维持运营。广告是无线电的生命线，但目前的广告收入极其微薄，且现有的广告价格低得可笑。实际上，有可能以每月 350 元（中国货币）的价格在一家主要电台获得每天一小时的时段，或者以低至每月 37.50 元的价格播放一则“插播”公告。这样的费率不可能指望在无线电广播中激发出任何惊人的原创性，或使电台有能力雇佣人才进行公共娱乐表演。由于收入不足，外资电台尤其必须几乎完全局限于播放唱片，最多只有一两名播音员和一名每日新闻评论员。构成大多数的中国电台在不同时间有演播室节目，但这些电台因控制和统制而变得如此无害，以至于它们的节目甚至对自己的民众也缺乏吸引力，后者的焦虑和愤慨使他们无心欣赏受审查的娱乐节目。

可能引起中国民众兴趣的节目，即那些通过短波从重庆国民政府电台传来的节目，一直受到警惕的日本人的拦截和“干扰”。然而，有时也会传来受欢迎的中文讨论，形式来自“流动”电台的节目，这些电台当然必须像在德国一样在此地保持隐蔽。这些是上海警觉的中国人自发创作的成果，构成了他们对国家斗争的贡献。在这些节目中，播放国歌，招募新兵，并传达国民政府及其领导人的目标和斗争。

两家日本电台 XQHA（630 kc）和 XOJB（900 ck）接受其政府的财政援助，因此本应能提供比现在更好的节目。但鉴于日本人在其他领域的所作所为，若要期望他们在通过无线电传播文化方面过分努力，未免太考验想象力了，特别是考虑到一个明显的事实，即日本电台像其他一切事物一样，处于军队当局的严密控制之下。

虽然东京在外务省设有“文化”局，并在海外传播日本文化方面花费巨资，但在此掌权的日本军阀对此类事情几乎没有或根本没有兴趣。

XQHA 电台确实重播一些它认为可能符合上海（及军队当局）口味的东京节目。其宣传和新闻均“调整”至此水平，不再更高。音乐几乎完全是唱片，尽管有时节目包括用日语演唱的德国和意大利歌剧。另一家主要的日本电台 XOJB 原是中国政府的大上海计划中心电台。被没收后，它成为日本军队在上海进行无线电宣传的总部，使用普通话、粤语和英语广播。与其他电台一样，其宣传形式为详尽的新闻，详细叙述那些奇迹般的

Jul 24, 1939
THE CHINA WEEKLY REVIEW
99

the Japanese army is accomplishing for the benefit of
the Chinese people, and how, through its heroic efforts,
the British and other foreigners have been restrained
from enslaving the entire Chinese population.
Needless to say, stations ZQHA and XOJB have
to pay their announcers more than most other stations,
for it is obviously a severe strain on the commentator's
conscience, especially since the Japanese stations require
that Chinese deliver to Chinese, and foreigners deliver
to foreigners full accounts of the Japanese "good will"
mission in China.
Besides those mouthpieces and a few other smaller
owned stations, which they have coerced into doing
their bidding, the Japanese have still another (unofficial)
spokesman, or spokeswoman rather, in the person of
Mrs. Bobertson, who broadcasts the news of the pro-
Japanese Shanghai Times over station ZQHA (820 kc),
owned and operated by Mrs. Robertson herself.
Two stations which cause Major Asano and his
Japanese Control Board more sleepless nights than all
the others put together, are stations XMHC and XMHA,
which are the most powerful stations in Shanghai. Both
are under American control and thus are outside the
jurisdiction of his "Control Board." Station XMHC
is owned by the Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury and ex-
presses the sympathetic Chinese policy of the paper in its
news broadcasts to a far greater public than the paper
could ever hope to reach. More deleterious to Japanese
military objectives is the fact that it broadcasts in Chinese
the news of its Chinese paper the Ta Mei Wan Pao, the
morning edition of which had been recently suspended
from publication by the S.M.C. as a result of Japanese
pressure, and police "appeasement."
Station XMHA is the property of an American,
U.S. Harkson, who is proprietor of the Henningsen
Produce Company, dealers in eggs, egg products, butter
and manufacturers of ice cream and confectionery.
The most provocative thing about this station, so far as
the Japanese are concerned, aside from the fact that they
do not control it, is the news broadcast of Carol Alcott.
As a news commentator he is by far the most popular
among the foreign population of Shanghai, and what
makes him popular among the foreigners and Chinese
makes him bitterly unpopular with the Japanese Control
Board and its Nipponese army supporters. The Japanese
claim that Alcott's broadcasts are "pro-British," and
as such are anathema to the Nipponese point of view.
Whether the Japanese will be able to finally get
Alcott off the air or curb his broadcasts remains to be
seen. Recently there have been rumors of trouble
between Alcott and the manager of the station who,
allegedly did not approve of some of Alcott's state-
ments. Several weeks ago the Japanese succeeded by
pressure, intimidation and chicanery in causing the Harkson
station to discontinue the broadcasts of The China Weekly
Review, whose weekly summaries of world news equalled
Alcott's daily news broadcasts in popularity among
both foreigners and Chinese. Several hundred protests,
more than 100 in writing, were received as a result of
the discontinuance of The Review's broadcast and as
a result, the manager of XMHA, fearing a loss in prestige
of his station, tried to induce the The Review to resume,
but subject to censorship as to its utterances. The
editor of The Review rejected this offer.
Since XMHA is the property of the Henningsen
interests and is primarily useful to them as an advertising
medium for their butter, ice cream and confectionery
products, it remains to be seen how far they may be wil-
ling to go in opposing Japanese control. The main Hen-
ningsen plant is said to be located in Japanese-controlled
territory, hence subject to military pressure.
The Henningsen station recently has been criticised
for its failure to re-broadcast here the independent news
and entertainment program of the famous Treasure
Island Station at San Francisco. The Treasure Island
Station (W6XBE) was constructed and is maintained
by the General Electric Company (without advertising)
for the purpose of maintaining American news and
cultural contacts with South American and Oriental
countries. Its broadcasts may be picked up here by
shortwave receivers between 7:30 A.M. and 11 A. M.,
and 8 P.M. to 11 P.M. If the programs were re-broad-
cast by a local station they could be heard by every owner
of a radio in east and central China.
It must be remembered of course, that radio, as an
instrument of propaganda is almost limitless, in comparison
with other agencies of communication. News and com-
ment which might not be so disastrous to the Japanese
interests in Shanghai, where practically everyone is of
the same mind concerning their invasion, might be
exceedingly inflammatory in those places where the
Japanese are struggling to keep out all the truth—that
truth which they have good reason to believe, might
prove to be as disastrous an invasion for their despotism,
as the one they had envisioned for China.
For entertainment, XHMC and XMHA depend up-
on recordings, giving the public anything from Beethoven
to the latest song hits, which are often quite a bit late
by the time they arrive in Shanghai. The Christian
Broadcasting Station, station XMHD (760 kc.) is devoted
almost exclusively to religious topics, with the exception
of news comments and occasional musical recordings.
Indeed if an embargo were ever placed on records, the
whole radio industry of Shanghai would collapse over-
night with a completeness that no strategy or edict of
the Japanese Control Board could ever hope to perform.
Not a single Shanghai station has had sufficient enter-
prise or ingenuity to build up its own programs as sta-
tions in the United States, even in small towns, have done.
The police Department of the S.M.C. has its own
station through which it directs the activities of its six
armoured volunteer cars and its dozen or so normal
radio vans, which patrol the streets. The S.M.C. it-
self also had in mind the erection of a radio station with
which to advance the music of its municipal orchestra,
but having allocated $200,000 for the orchestra and
only $3000 or so for the radio, all logical accountancy,
I suppose, collapsed at this point, and with it the broad-
casting project.
Thus into the surcharged air of Shanghai, goes
all the confusing network of sound, all the secret code
messages and dispatches from the private stations of the
various consulates, and military headquarters, the buz-
zing and interceptions of the Japanese, and so forth.
Shanghai is said to have more radio stations than any
other city in the world, a fact that one can prove any-
time by simply spinning the dial of his radio.
Today, radio in Shanghai as at present constituted
can see little or nothing, now or in the future, but a dreary
prospect, and cannot fail but reflect the anxiety and ten-
sion of these hectic days. And even those stations beyond
control of the Japanese Control Board, XMHA and
XMHC, in a position to give this city and the
other cities of China which they cover, outspoken views
and facts, may soon have to face a new dilemma and
persecution. Already the Japanese have in the process
of construction two kilowatt transmitters, now half
completed, and probably ready for operation next month.
These transmitters, allegedly were designed exclusively
to jam XMHA and XMHC off the air permanently,
if they choose to ignore the Control Board's last and
final ultimatum.
The real test will come when the Japanese seriously
try to force Alcott off the air as they succeeded in doing
with The China Weekly Review's weekly summary of world
news. Up to the present Alcott, who also is Shanghai's
best police reporter, has had S.M.P. support, although
a Japanese terrorist once threw a bomb against the front
door of XMHC while he was broadcasting and black-
mailers have written him numerous threatening letters.

1939年7月24日
《密勒氏评论报》
99

日军正在为中国人民的福祉而成就大业，以及它如何通过英勇努力，遏制了英国人和其他外国人奴役全体中国人口的企图。
不用说，ZQHA和XOJB电台不得不向其播音员支付高于大多数其他电台的薪酬，因为这对评论员的良心显然是一种严峻的考验，尤其是因为日方电台要求中国人向中国人、外国人向外国人全面传达日本在华“善意”使命的内容。
除了那些喉舌机构以及少数几家被胁迫听命于它们的小型私营电台外，日本人还有另一位（非官方的）代言人，或者更确切地说是女代言人，即罗伯逊夫人（Mrs. Bobertson (音译)），她通过ZQHA电台（820千周）广播亲日的《上海泰晤士报》的新闻，该电台由罗伯逊夫人本人拥有并运营。
令浅野少佐（Major Asano (音译)）及其日本管制委员会比其他所有情况加起来都更加失眠的两家电台，是XMHC和XMHA电台，它们是上海功率最大的两家电台。两者均受美国人控制，因此不在其“管制委员会”的管辖范围之内。XMHC电台由《上海晚邮报与水星报》（Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury）拥有，并在其新闻广播中表达该报同情中国的政策，其受众范围远超该报本身所能企及。对日军军事目标更具破坏性的是，该电台用中文广播其中文报纸《大美晚报》的新闻，该报的晨版近期因日本人的压力和工部局警务处的“绥靖”而被停刊。
XMHA电台是一位美国人U.S. Harkson (音译) 的财产，他是亨宁森农产品公司（Henningsen Produce Company）的所有者，该公司经销鸡蛋、蛋制品、黄油，并制造冰淇淋和糖果。就日本人而言，这家电台最具挑衅性的地方，除了他们无法控制它这一事实外，还在于卡罗尔·奥尔科特（Carol Alcott (音译)）的新闻广播。作为一名新闻评论员，他在上海外籍人口中极受欢迎，而使他受到外国人和中国人欢迎的因素，也使他遭到日本管制委员会及其日本军队支持者的强烈憎恶。日本人声称奥尔科特的广播“亲英”，因此为日本人的观点所不容。
日本人最终能否让奥尔科特停播或限制其广播，仍有待观察。最近有传言称奥尔科特与电台经理之间发生纠纷，据称经理不赞同奥尔科特的某些言论。几周前，日本人通过施压、恐吓和欺诈手段，迫使哈克森（Harkson）电台停止广播《密勒氏评论报》，该报的世界新闻每周摘要在外国人和中国人中的受欢迎程度堪比奥尔科特的每日新闻广播。由于停播《评论报》的广播，收到了数百起抗议，其中书面抗议超过100起，因此，XMHA电台经理担心电台声誉受损，试图诱导《评论报》恢复广播，但要求其言论接受审查。《评论报》编辑拒绝了这一提议。
由于XMHA电台属于亨宁森财团（Henningsen interests）的财产，且主要作为其黄油、冰淇淋和糖果产品的广告媒介对其有用，因此他们在反对日本控制方面愿意走多远，仍有待观察。据悉，亨宁森的主要工厂位于日本控制的领土内，因此易受军事压力影响。
亨宁森电台最近因其未能在此重播旧金山著名的宝藏岛电台（Treasure Island Station）的独立新闻和娱乐节目而受到批评。宝藏岛电台（W6XBE）由通用电气公司（General Electric Company）建造并维护（无广告），旨在维持美国与南美及东方国家的新闻和文化联系。其广播可在上午7:30至11:00以及晚上8:00至11:00之间通过短波接收机在此收听到。如果由本地电台重播这些节目，中国东部和中部地区的每一位收音机所有者都能听到。
当然，必须记住，与其他传播机构相比，无线电作为宣传工具几乎是无限的。在上海，几乎所有人都对日本的入侵持相同看法，某些新闻和评论可能对日本利益造成的灾难性后果并不那么严重，但在那些日本人竭力封锁一切真相的地方，这些内容可能极具煽动性——他们有充分理由相信，这种真相的传播对其专制统治来说，可能证明是一场与其曾设想加诸中国的那场入侵同样灾难性的入侵。
在娱乐方面，XHMC和XMHA依赖唱片，向公众提供从贝多芬到最新流行歌曲的各种内容，这些歌曲传到上海时往往已经滞后不少。基督教广播电台，即XMHD电台（760千周），几乎专门致力于宗教题材，例外情况仅有新闻评论和偶尔的音乐唱片播放。的确，如果对唱片实施禁运，整个上海无线电行业将一夜之间彻底崩溃，其彻底程度是日本管制委员会的任何策略或法令都无法企及的。没有一家上海电台具备足够的进取心或独创性来建立自己的节目，就像美国甚至小城镇的电台所做的那样。
工部局警务处拥有自己的电台，通过该电台指挥其六辆装甲志愿警车和十几辆普通无线电巡逻车的活动，这些车辆在街道上巡逻。工部局本身也曾考虑建立一座广播电台，以推广其市立管弦乐队的音乐，但在为管弦乐队拨款20万美元，而仅为无线电项目拨款约3,000美元之后，我想，所有合理的会计核算在此刻都崩溃了，广播计划也随之夭折。
因此，在上海充满张力的空气中，充斥着所有令人困惑的声音网络，来自各领事馆和军事总部私人电台的所有秘密代码信息和电报，日本人的嗡嗡干扰和拦截等等。据说上海的广播电台数量比世界上任何其他城市都多，任何人只需旋转收音机的调谐旋钮即可随时证实这一事实。
目前上海构成的无线电状况，无论现在还是将来，都看不到什么希望，前景黯淡，不可避免地反映出这些动荡日子中的焦虑和紧张。即使是那些不受日本管制委员会控制的电台，如XMHA和XMHC，本有能力向这座城市及其覆盖的中国其他城市提供坦率的观点和事实，也可能很快面临新的困境和迫害。日本人已经在建造两台千瓦发射机，目前已完成一半，可能下个月即可投入运行。据称，如果这些电台选择无视管制委员会的最后通牒，这些发射机将专门用于永久干扰XMHA和XMHA电台，使其停播。
真正的考验将是当日本人认真试图迫使奥尔科特停播时，正如他们成功迫使《密勒氏评论报》的世界新闻每周摘要停播一样。到目前为止，奥尔科特也是上海最好的警务记者，一直得到工部局警务处的支持，尽管一名日本恐怖分子曾在他广播期间向XMHC电台的前门投掷炸弹，勒索者也给他写过许多恐吓信。

THE CHINA WEEKLY REVIEW
June 24, 1939

Japan Coordinates Tientsin Blockade With Hitler's
Preparations to Liquidate Danzig Problem

WITH the Japanese blockade of the foreign Con-
cessions in Tientsin well into its second week,
with no signs of yielding on either side, and
with the tension between Japan and the European demo-
cratic powers growing from day to day, it becomes
necessary to weigh up the implications of the new Far
Eastern situation which Japan has produced by her latest
actions and to consider it in relation to the whole current
complex of international rivalries.

There no longer exists the slightest doubt that what
we are now witnessing is the operation of the secret
German-Japanese agreement which lies behind the so-
called anti-Comintern Pact, for the Japanese action in
Tientsin has coincided with a series
of German moves which indicate an
intent to "settle" the Danzig question
at an early date. As we have
indicated several times before, an
attempt by Germany to secure
control over Danzig, especially if
Poland makes good on her oft-
repeated determination to resist the
reincorporation of the Free City into
the Reich, carries with it the imminent
threat of a general European war.
In the face of such a threat, the hands
of Britain and France would be tied
in the Far East, while the United
States would probably have to choose
between aiding the European democra-
cies against Germany and holding
off Japan in the Far East.

It is because of the growingly
strained relations between Germany
and Poland that Japan feels she can
act with impunity. Contrariwise, the
Japanese action in Tientsin is bolster-
ing Germany in her determination to
secure Danzig—even, perhaps, at the
risk of plunging Europe into war.
That Germany and Japan are consciously and
deliberately coordinating their actions in their
respective spheres is as clear as anything could be.
Both hope to profit from a situation which makes it
difficult for the democracies to erect an effective barrier
against Germany in the West or Japan in the East.

REPORTS from Europe this week show that Britain
and Soviet Russia are as far from an agreement as
ever. Indeed, there appears to be ample ground
for the assertion that the project for a triple alliance to
embrace Britain, France and Soviet Russia is dead and
now only awaits the ministrations of the diplomatic
undertakers. For weeks, Soviet insistence on guarantees
to the Baltic states was the apparent obstacle to an agree-
ment. Late last week it appeared that Britain was pre-
pared to concede this Soviet demand. This week there
have been indications that Moscow is demanding a
guarantee against Japan in the Far East as the price of
an agreement with the Western democracies.

If this is actually the case, there is only one con-
struction to be placed on the Soviet attitude, namely, that
Moscow is not desirous of tying itself to the democracies
and is putting forward demands which the prospective
allies cannot be expected to concede, with the well-formed
intention of preventing any agreement. The question
will be asked: Why, then, does not Moscow openly
break off negotiations? The answer is very simple.
A definite rupture of the Anglo-Soviet parleys would

decrease Moscow's bargaining powers with Berlin, with
which the Kremlin hopes to reach an agreement holding
all those advantages which the democracies are not able
to offer. And so the diplomatic farce is likely to be
played through to the last act.

The economic advantages to both Germany and
Soviet Russia which could be expected to flow from a
definitive agreement have been stated too often to require
reassertion. Equally obvious are the strategic gains to
be made. For Russia, the gains would be enormous.
First of all, the Nazi war threat against the Soviet Union
—haunting nightmare of Kremlin dreams for more than
six years—would be exorcised for at least a considerable

spell. Secondly—and this is no mean consideration,
either—Japan would lose her one valuable ally in Europe
and Moscow could face Dai Nippon in the Far East
without the fear of possible military embarrassment on
the Western frontiers of the Soviet Union.

For Nazi Germany, the political advantages of an
agreement with Soviet Russia are equally great. Russia
and Germany in combination would represent the most
formidable military combination Europe has ever seen.
Russia, of course, has no aggressive aims in Europe, and
most likely would not become a party to any which
Germany might entertain. But even if Russia is just
"neutralized," the hands of Hitler would be so streng-
thened as to enable him to tackle with downright earnest-
ness the never-abandoned task of getting back Germany's
old colonies—with perhaps a few new ones as well.

No wonder Prime Minister Chamberlain is begin-
ning to talk once more in the language of "appeasement"
—and no wonder Japan is so alarmed by the prospect
of Soviet-German rapprochement!

There appears to be one especially important ques-
tion unanswered at the present time: How long can
Moscow string her suitors along without coming to a
definite decision? That remains to be seen.

THE question which immediately interests foreigners
in China is what, if anything, the Western demo-
cracies intend to do to counteract, and if possible
terminate, the intolerable pressure to which the Japanese

《密勒氏评论报》
1939年6月24日

日本协调天津封锁行动与希特勒解决但泽问题的准备工作

随着日本对外国在天津租界的封锁进入第二周，双方均无让步迹象，且日本与欧洲民主国家之间的紧张关系日益加剧，因此有必要权衡日本最新行动所造成的远东新局势之含义，并将其置于当前复杂的国际竞争整体背景下加以考量。

毫无疑问，我们目前所目睹的正是隐藏在所谓《反共产国际协定》背后的德日秘密协定的运作，因为日本在天津的行动恰好与德国的一系列举动相吻合，这些举动表明德国有意尽早“解决”但泽问题。正如我们此前多次指出的那样，德国试图控制但泽，特别是如果波兰坚持其屡次重申的决心、抵抗将自由市重新并入帝国，这将带来爆发全面欧洲战争的迫在眉睫的威胁。面对这种威胁，英国和法国在远东的手脚将被束缚，而美国可能不得不在援助欧洲民主国家对抗日德与在远东遏制日本之间做出选择。

正是因为德波关系日益紧张，日本才觉得自己可以肆无忌惮地采取行动。反之，日本在天津的行动也加强了德国确保获得但泽的决心——甚至不惜冒着使欧洲陷入战争的风险。德国和日本有意识且故意地在各自势力范围内协调行动，这一点已再清楚不过。双方都希望从一种令民主国家难以在西方针对德国或在东方针对日本建立有效屏障的局势中获利。

本周来自欧洲的报道显示，英国与苏俄距离达成协议仍像以往一样遥远。事实上，似乎有充分理由断言，旨在囊括英国、法国和苏俄的三国同盟计划已经夭折，现在只待外交殓葬者来处理后事。数周以来，苏联坚持要求对波罗的海国家提供保证，这似乎是达成协议的明显障碍。上周晚些时候，英国似乎准备让步以满足苏联的这一要求。本周有迹象表明，莫斯科要求作为与西方民主国家达成协议的条件，必须提供针对日本在远东行动的保证。

如果情况确实如此，那么对苏联的态度只能有一种解释，即莫斯科并不希望将自己与民主国家捆绑在一起，而是提出预期盟友不可能接受的的要求，其意图明确，旨在阻止任何协议的达成。人们会问：既然如此，莫斯科为何不公开中断谈判？答案很简单。英苏会谈的明确破裂将

削弱莫斯科在与柏林谈判时的筹码，克里姆林宫希望与柏林达成一项协议，以获得民主国家无法提供的各种优势。因此，这场外交闹剧很可能会演到最后一幕。

德苏两国若达成正式协议所能带来的经济利益已被反复陈述，无需赘述。同样明显的还有战略上的收益。对俄罗斯而言，收益将是巨大的。首先，纳粹对苏联的战争威胁——困扰克里姆林宫梦境长达六年多的噩梦——将在相当长的一段时间内被驱除。

左翼刊物如何看待这一局势

[漫画说明]：
苏联的安全
“那些绅士们不会喜欢我这样做！”
“把救生圈扔给我！”
征兵
欧洲的和平
《伦敦论坛报》

其次——这绝非微不足道的考虑——日本将失去其在欧洲唯一的宝贵盟友，莫斯科在远东面对大日本帝国时，将不必担心苏联西部边境可能出现的军事困境。

对纳粹德国而言，与苏俄达成协议的政治优势同样巨大。俄德结合将代表欧洲有史以来最强大的军事组合。当然，俄罗斯在欧洲没有侵略意图，很可能也不会参与德国可能怀有的任何侵略计划。但即使俄罗斯只是被“中立化”，希特勒的手脚也将得到极大加强，使他能够认真着手处理从未放弃的任务，即收回德国的旧殖民地——或许还包括一些新的殖民地。

难怪张伯伦首相又开始使用“绥靖”的口吻说话——也难怪日本对苏德接近的前景感到如此惊恐！

目前似乎有一个尤其重要的问题尚未得到解答：莫斯科能在不做出明确决定的情况下，将其追求者拖延多久？这还有待观察。

在华外国人立即关心的问题是，西方民主国家打算采取什么措施（如果有的话）来抵消，并尽可能终止日本施加的难以忍受的压力

Date December 22, 1938.
(印：SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE S. B. REGISTRY No. 36)
Subject Broadcasts of anti-Japanese and National Salvation Nature
- action taken by Municipal Police.
Made by D.S.I. Logan Forwarded by C. Crawford D.I.

With reference to the remarks of the Commissioner
of Police appended to Special Branch Report, dated December
17, 1938, on the subject of broadcasting stations and the
Japanese Broadcasting Superintendence Office, the following
is a brief summary of instances of national salvation and
anti-Japanese propaganda broadcast from Broadcasting
Stations in the Settlement, culled from Special Branch
reports, and the action taken by the Municipal Police :-
D 7406/1
1. On three occasions in May and June, 1937, the Yung Zoe
Dramatic Society, Lane 230, 8 Amoy Road, broadcast plays
of a national salvation nature through the Shanghai
Station of the Ministry of Communications, then located
in the Sassoon House. Special Branch staff listened-
in to the broadcast, but no action was taken.
D 8014
2. In September, 1937, the Shanghai Amusement Circles
National Salvation Association (defunct), Lane 880, 5
Avenue Edward VII, made arrangements to broadcast
lectures bearing on the commemoration of the September
18 Anniversary, for one week from September 18, 1937,
from the Tung Fang Station (XHHG) which was loaned to
the above association by order of the Bureau of Social
Affairs. Liu Tsung-san (刘春山), a comedian and
committee member of the association in question, was
informed by the Police on September 17 that the broadcasts
arranged would not be allowed if propaganda was to be
included in the speeches, and that should such be found
to be the case the station would be closed down. As
a result of the warning, the broadcasts did not take
place.

主题 关于反日及救国性质广播
- 工部局警务处采取的行动。
由 D.S.I. Logan 撰写 由 C. Crawford D.I. 转呈

鉴于警务总监在1938年12月17日关于广播电台及日本广播监理办公室事宜的特别处报告后所附评语，以下简要总结从特别处报告中摘录的租界内广播电台播出的救国及反日宣传实例，以及工部局警务处采取的行动：-
D 7406/1
1. 1937年5月和6月间，位于厦门路230弄的永浙剧社通过当时设在沙逊大厦的交通部上海电台播出了具有救国性质的剧目。特别处人员监听了广播，但未采取行动。
D 8014
2. 1937年9月，位于爱多亚路880弄的上海游艺界救国会（已解散）安排从1937年9月18日起的一周内，通过东方电台 (XHHG) 播出纪念九一八周年的讲座，该电台系奉社会局命令借予上述协会使用。刘春山 (Liu Tsung-san)，一位喜剧演员及该协会委员，于9月17日接到警方通知，如果演讲中包含宣传内容，则不允许进行安排的广播，一旦发现此类情况，电台将被关闭。由于受到警告，广播未能进行。

3. Hwa Shing Broadcasting Station, 19 Tsingtao Road
    On October 6, 1937, songs of a national salvation
nature were broadcast from this station. In accordance
with the instructions of the D.C. (Special Branch) reading:
    "Warn Mr. Yen that if the protection afforded by the
Settlement is abused the Station will be closed down.
News items and reasonable propaganda may be permitted
but abusive terms and songs banned will not; further
programmes will be submitted in advance to Special
Branch."
    Mr. Yen Tuh-yih (顏得一) who was in charge of the Hwa
Shing Station and of the Shanghai Chorus and Dramatic
Group, responsible for the broadcasts mentioned, was
called to Special Branch on October 8 and warned in
terms of the above instruction. Later, on three occasions,
Mr. Yen submitted a number of songs which were to be
broadcast, to the Special Branch for censorship. A number
of the songs were ordered to be deleted by the Municipal
Police for being of a national salvation or anti-
Japanese nature.

4. Great China Dispensary Broadcasting Station
    On October 22, 23 and 24, 1937 national salvation
songs were heard from this station. The manager of the
station was warned on October 28, 1937, that further
broadcasting of banned songs, plays of an objectionable
nature or any other items that savoured of anti-Japanese
propaganda would entail closure of the station. Songs
were later submitted to Special Branch for censorship
and those found to be of an objectionable nature ordered
to be deleted.

3. 华兴广播电台，青岛路19号
    1937年10月6日，该电台播出了具有救国性质的歌曲。根据特别处副总监的指示：
    “警告颜先生，如果滥用租界提供的保护，电台将被关闭。新闻项目和合理的宣传或许被允许，但辱骂性言辞和被禁歌曲则不行；后续节目需提前提交特别处审查。”
    负责华兴电台及负责上述广播的上海合唱戏剧团的颜得一 (Yen Tuh-yih) 先生于10月8日被召至特别处，并按上述指示受到警告。此后，颜先生三次向特别处提交拟广播的歌曲以供审查。工部局警务处下令删除其中若干首具有救国或反日性质的歌曲。

4. 大华药房广播电台
    1937年10月22日、23日和24日，从该电台听到救国歌曲。1937年10月28日，电台经理受到警告，若继续播放被禁歌曲、性质令人反感的剧目或任何其他带有反日宣传意味的项目，将导致电台关闭。随后歌曲被提交特别处审查，凡发现性质令人反感者，均被责令删除。

Japanese hostilities in August, 1937, the registration
and control of commercial radio broadcasting stations in
Shanghai was vested in the Ministry of Communications of
the National Government of China. In December, 1936, a
Board of Censorship for the control of programmes was
established in Room 537, 5th floor, Continental Emporium
Building, Nanking Road, and was assisted by representatives
of the Ministry of Communications who had an office in
Telegraph Office, 200 Szechuen Road. At the time in
question, there existed in Shanghai two Chinese Government
stations, thirty-five Chinese privately owned commercial
broadcasting stations and five similar stations owned
by foreigners. Before August, 1937, nine of the Chinese
stations were closed by order of the Ministry of
Communications for contravening the regulations of the
latter authority.

Following the outbreak of Sino-Japanese hostilities,
Chinese radio stations injected into their commercial
programmes considerable anti-Japanese matter but
as a result of police action coupled with the withdrawal
of Chinese troops from Shanghai such propaganda ceased.

During March, 1938, the Japanese Army Authorities
formed an organ calculated to assume the registration and
control of broadcasting stations, formerly exercised by
the National Government, with a temporary office in Room 220 of

On April 27, Major Asano of the Broadcasting
Superintendence Office addressed a letter to the Secretary-
General, S.M.C., announcing that his Office had taken over
the supervision of broadcasting stations and all affairs
connected with the control of broadcasting. The letter
gave an account of his efforts to secure control by means
of registering the stations and referred to the circulation
of "Instruction Memos. Nos. 1, 2 and 3." It also mentioned
that the stations failed to register and that :

" In the above circumstances, we are now compelled
"to ready to stop the business of those, who break the
"regulations by a some compulsory means, such as to
"remove or to break down some important parts of machine."
(copy of the letter is attached as Appendix "D")

The above letter was discussed by the Commissioner
of Police and Secretary-General, S.M.C., on April 27, 1938, when
it was felt that direct action by the Japanese in the Settlement
should be avoided. Instructions were then issued whereby
D.S.I. Logan was detailed to call upon Major Asano and propose
that the Police would obtain completed registration forms
from Chinese Broadcasting Stations (vide Commissioner of
Police's memo. dated April 27, 1938 - copy attached as
Appendix "E").

At 3 p.m. April 27, 1938, D.S.I. Logan and D.S.
Kamashita visited the Broadcasting Superintendence Office

consequently the proposals outlined above were made to Mr.
Y. Ban, Major Asano's deputy. It was suggested to Mr. Ban
that he should supply the forms of application for registration
to the Police who would undertake to deliver them to the
different Chinese broadcasting stations and, after the
necessary details had been filled in, collect and forward
them to the Broadcasting Superintendence Office. The
suggestion was at first coldly received by Mr. Ban, who
appeared to hold the view that as the stations had ignored
all the notifications sent out by the Japanese on the subject,
they had deprived themselves of any further consideration
and should be treated accordingly, in other words, forced
to cease broadcasting. Later, however, he modified his
attitude and expressed himself as being satisfied with the
form which the Police assistance was to take but stated that

Major Asano expressed his satisfaction at the action taken

would not exceed the form of control exercised by the
Kuomintang Government, except in so far as anti-Japanese
propaganda and matter harmful to the Japanese forces is
concerned.
It should be mentioned that on April 28, 1938, due
to nervousness as to what action would be taken by the
Japanese, all unregistered stations ceased broadcasting,
temporarily. However, confidence was somewhat restored
after a lapse of three or four days and on May 2, 1938, a
total of eight Chinese stations had resumed broadcasting.

On December 8, 1938, a letter was received from
the Yeu Lien (Union) Station (XHHV) announcing that this
station would commence broadcasting on December 10, 1938,
on a wavelength of K.C.780 (the wavelength adopted by
Mr. Vanmeter). Enclosed in the letter was a permit,
dated 30.11.38, issued by Major Asano authorising the
Station to use K.C.780.
It should be mentioned that the Yeu Lien Station,
which formerly operated on a permit issued by the Ministry
of Communications, over a wavelength of K.C.880, voluntarily
closed down in May, 1938. On October 3, 1938, the station
applied to the Police for permission to re-open when, due
to the understanding between the Police and the Broadcasting
Superintendence Office concerning new stations, arrived at
in May, 1938, referred to earlier in this report, permission
to re-open was withheld until such time as the station
should obtain the sanction of the Broadcasting Superintendence
Office. The management of the Yeu Lien Station, however,
stated that they would not recognize the latter and nothing
further was heard from them till the receipt of the letter
dated December 8, 1938, mentioned above. It would appear
that some agreement was arrived at in the meantime between
the station and the Japanese, the latter making a condition
of the granting of permission to re-open, that the station
instead of using K.C.880 (formerly used by this station and
which as far as is known is still vacant) should broadcast
over K.C.780 in order to embarrass Mr. Vanmeter.

1938年12月8日，警方收到友联电台（Yeu Lien (Union) Station, XHHV）来信，宣布该电台将于1938年12月10日以 K.C.780 波长（即 Vanmeter 先生采用的波长）开始广播。信中附有一份由浅野大佐（Major Asano）于1938年11月30日签发的许可证，授权该电台使用 K.C.780。
需要提及的是，友联电台此前持交通部颁发的许可证，以 K.C.880 波长运营，于1938年5月自愿停播。1938年10月3日，该电台向警方申请重新开播，但由于警方与广播监理所之间就新电台事宜达成的谅解（本报告前文提及，达成于1938年5月），在该电台获得广播监理所批准之前，暂缓批准其重新开播。然而，友联电台管理层表示他们不承认后者，直到收到上述1938年12月8日的信件之前，未再有任何消息。看来在此期间，该电台与日方达成了某种协议，日方将重新开播许可的条件设定为：该电台不得使用 K.C.880（该电台以前使用的频率，据所知目前仍空闲），而必须使用 K.C.780 进行广播，以便给 Vanmeter 先生制造麻烦。

On December 10, 1938, Major Asano addressed a letter to the Police requesting the latter to issue the necessary permission to the Yeu Lien Station to operate on K.C. 780 and intimating that the Superintendence Office had installed a machine in the Yeu Lien Station "for the purpose of castigating Mr. Vanmeter's Station by means of broadcasting a special wave."

It has also been learned that Mr. Vanmeter had addressed a letter to the Yeu Lien Station threatening the institution of legal proceedings against the latter for encroachment on the right of the former to use K.C.780.

From the foregoing it is plain that the Japanese are determined to secure control of the broadcasting situation locally, irrespective of the rights of old established stations owned by Chinese and of the rights of foreigners enjoying extra-territorial privileges.

The position is complicated further by the fact that technically, the right to control radio stations is vested in the National Government. Further, the right of the Japanese to take over control of broadcasting in the Settlement has not been recognized either by the S.M.C. or by the Governments of the various countries having extra-territorial rights in China.

The situation has now reached a point where, unless some clarification of the situation is obtained, the greatest confusion is likely to develop with the possibility of incidents affecting law and order.

(To Dr.)
D.C. (Special Branch)

Wrogan
D. S. I.

1938年12月10日，浅野大佐致信警方，请求警方颁发必要许可，允许友联电台在 K.C. 780 上运营，并暗示监理所已在友联电台安装了一台机器，“目的是通过发射特殊电波来惩罚 Vanmeter 先生的电台”。
另获悉，Vanmeter 先生曾致信友联电台，威胁就该电台侵犯其使用 K.C.780 的权利提起法律诉讼。
综上所述，显而易见，日方决心掌控当地的广播局势，而不顾华人拥有的老牌电台的权利以及享有治外法权的外国人的权利。
鉴于技术上控制广播电台的权利属于国民政府，局势变得更为复杂。此外，工部局（S.M.C.）或在中国拥有治外法权的各国政府均未承认日方接管租界内广播控制权的权利。
目前局势已发展到这样的地步：除非对局势加以澄清，否则极有可能出现最大的混乱，并可能发生影响治安的事件。
